The leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix splits the nodes by sign at that edge, and neither side splits further, giving two communities drawn in the accent color and teal: 0 is D, E, F, G and 1 is A, B, C." width="100%"} Spectral optimization method using recursive bisection based on the leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix. Splits communities hierarchically when modularity improves. Best for medium-sized graphs (< 20K nodes) with clear 2-way divisions and hierarchical structure. The algorithm starts with every node in one community. It computes the leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix for that group and splits the nodes by the sign of their entry in the vector. Each half is then split again in the same way, and a group is left whole as soon as no split would increase modularity. You never choose the number of communities; it falls out of where splitting stops. Reach for this method when you want: - a deterministic partition (no random seed involved) that is reproducible between runs - a top-down, divisive view of structure, where the first split is the most important division in the network - a spectral alternative to compare against agglomerative methods such as `cmty_fast_greedy()` or `cmty_louvain()` The graph must be undirected and edge weights are ignored (every edge counts once). An edgeless graph puts every node in its own community, and an empty graph gives an empty result. The community assignments are always written to the node DataFrame, even when `return_dict=True`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store community assignments in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `cmty_l_eigenvec`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to community IDs (0-indexed, contiguous). The numbers are arbitrary labels: only whether two nodes share a number is meaningful. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If graph is directed (requires undirected graph). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Newman (2006) recast community detection as a linear-algebra problem: the modularity matrix $B_{ij} = A_{ij} - \dfrac{k_i k_j}{2m}$ measures each edge's contribution to modularity relative to a null model, and its leading eigenvector defines the split that gains the most modularity in one binary cut. The implementation finds that eigenvector by power iteration, partitions nodes by sign, and recurses on each side, refusing to split whenever doing so would lower modularity. Each split costs $O(n^2)$, and the recursion terminates only when the structure genuinely has hierarchical two-way divisions, so the final community count can be smaller than what agglomerative methods produce. Use `cmty_fast_greedy()` or `cmty_louvain()` beyond a few tens of thousands of nodes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The eigenvector split finds the natural division at the bridge edge, giving each triangle its own community: ::: {#979a4336 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) # Build two complete triangles graph.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), # Bridge ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")]) communities = graph.cmty_l_eigenvec(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): cid for nid, cid in communities.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'C': 0, 'A': 0, 'E': 1, 'F': 1, 'D': 1, 'B': 0} ``` ::: ::: Storing the result as a node attribute and chaining into `colorize_node_attrs()` visualizes the communities directly: ::: {#c4a166c0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")]) ) ( graph .cmty_l_eigenvec(attr_name="community") .colorize_node_attrs(node_attr_from="community", palette="Spectral") .describe() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of nodes : 6 Number of edges : 7 Directed : False Density : 0.47 Average degree (min, max) : 2.33 (2, 3) Connected : True Number of connected components : 1 Tree : False Bipartite : False Computations: - cmty_l_eigenvec() -> attr: 'community' (6 of 6 nodes) Node aesthetics: - color <- community via colorize (palette: "Spectral") (values: #d53e4f, #f46d43, 6 of 6 nodes) ``` ::: ::: On Zachary's karate club, recursive bisection goes beyond the famous two-faction split and settles on four communities. Counting the members of each shows their sizes: ::: {#ba29e5c9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter karate = ec.karate_club() communities = karate.cmty_l_eigenvec(return_dict=True) sorted(Counter(communities.values()).items()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [(0, 9), (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 12)] ``` ::: :::
